facts.fact: Described in 2014 by Keith, Hadiaty, Busson and Hubert in the journal Cybium (38(3): 173–178).
It is a sicydiine goby in the amphidromous genus Sicyopus.
In both sexes the first dorsal fin has five spines.
The second dorsal fin and the anal fin each have one spine and nine segmented rays.
Males have a distinctive body colour that helps tell the species apart from other Sicyopus.
The name refers to the fish's bright red throat and belly.
The body is elongated, with 15 pectoral-fin rays and 10–12 scales in a zigzag series.
It has not been evaluated for the IUCN Red List.
Adults have a very slender body.
It is known from Java and Bali in Indonesia.
The type specimens were collected in streams on Java and Bali.
It is a tropical freshwater fish that lives on the bottom.
Sicyopus gobies live in streams with clear, clean, running water.
It reaches the aquarium trade in shipments from Indonesia.
It hunts shrimp and fish fry, so it is a poor choice for tanks where cherry shrimp or livebearers such as guppies and endlers are being bred.
Getting wild fish to accept non-live foods can be hard. The video keepers lost almost half of their first group of 20.
Give it clear, clean, flowing water with hiding places and a sandy bottom.
It is a predator, not a grazer, and does not feed on aufwuchs or biofilm the way Stiphodon and Sicyopterus do.
It takes fairly large prey, including very small fish and shrimp up to about 1 cm long.
In the aquarium it hunted shrimp and endler fry, and sometimes ate fully grown cherry shrimp.
At first it refused dry food, frozen food and microworms. Over time it can be weaned onto flakes, granules and frozen foods.
It is a small micro-predator that chases anything that fits in its mouth.
Its colours reflect social rank: subordinate males are duller than the dominant male, perhaps to avoid provoking him.
Mature males have orangey-red lips, and the colour extends along about half the body toward the tail fin. Females are much duller.
Fully coloured males are orange with bright orange lips and no black stripe under the eye. Females are almost colourless.
Females grow slightly larger: 5.0 cm SL, against 4.7 cm SL for males.
In aquaria it spawns regularly, laying its eggs in caves.
The larvae are very tiny and develop in the sea. No hobbyist has reported rearing them successfully.

care.quote: Max length : 4.7 cm SL male/unsexed; 5.0 cm SL (female)
